content: Prepatellar bursitis, also referred to as housemaid's knee, is a condition characterized by swelling and pain localized above the patella (kneecap). This condition arises due to inflammation of the prepatellar bursa, a superficial bursa with a thin synovial lining situated between the skin and the patella. The prepatellar bursa typically develops during the early years of life as a result of mechanical pressure and friction. Its primary function is to reduce friction on underlying structures and facilitate maximal range of motion in the knee joint. Aseptic prepatellar bursitis is commonly caused by repetitive activities that involve prolonged kneeling, which is why it is colloquially known as housemaid's knee. In contrast, septic prepatellar bursitis, which is caused by bacterial infection, is more frequently observed in children and immunocompromised individuals. Overall, prepatellar bursitis is more prevalent in men than in women. On physical examination, prepatellar bursitis may present with redness and swelling of the prepatellar bursa. In cases of bacterial infection, inflammation and edema can lead to desquamation of the overlying skin. Severe cases may exhibit extensive redness and swelling involving the prepatellar bursa. Infrapatellar bursitis, which affects the infrapatellar bursa, can also present with similar findings, such as redness and swelling, but it occurs below the patella. It is essential to differentiate prepatellar bursitis from other causes of bursitis during the diagnostic process. Aseptic bursitis is typically managed conservatively. Treatment may include rest, ice application, and compression. In more complicated cases, oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or corticosteroid injections may be administered, provided that infection has been ruled out. Surgical excision of the bursa is rarely required. However, if the underlying cause of acute bursitis is not identified and addressed, the condition may progress to a chronic issue.
